items.body: "الليوث" حققوا انتصارًا تاريخيًا عبر السنغالي موري دياو، حارس مرمى الشباب، عن عدم رضاه عن مباراة الكلاسيكو المصغر ضد الغريم التقليدي الأهلي بدوري روشن السعودي، رغم الفوز العريض الذي حققه "الليوث". وفاز الشباب على الأهلي بنتيجة 6-1، خلال المباراة التي جمعت بينهما مساء الجمعة ، على ملعب إس إتش جي أرينا بالعاصمة السعودية الرياض، في الجولة الثانية عشرة من منافسات دوري روشن. وقال دياو في تصريحات لصحيفة "الشرق الأوسط" السعودية بعد المباراة: "نعمل بجد من أجل تحقيق الفوز في كل مباراة، وسنسعى إلى الانتصار في مواجهتنا المقبلة التي تسبق فترة التوقف". ويحل الشباب ضيفًا على أبها، يوم الخميس المقبل، في الجولة الثالثة عشرة من منافسات دوري روشن السعودي. تذاكر مباريات دوري روشن السعودي اشتر تذكرتك الآن! وأضاف الحارس السنغالي: "لست راضيًا بنسبة 100% عن المباراة، لأننا استقبلنا هدفًا، لكن الأهم في النهاية هو الحصول على النقاط الثلاثة". وسجل فراس البريكان هدف الأهلي الوحيد في الدقيقة 40 من عمر المباراة، بعدما تلقى عرضية أرضية حولها إلى داخل شباك موري دياو. 🎙️ | موري دياو حارس #الشباب يتحدث لـ«الشرق الأوسط»: - نعمل بجد من أجل تحقيق الفوز في كل مباراة، وسنسعى لإنهاء المواجهة المقبلة قبل فترة التوقف بالانتصار. - لست راضياً بنسبة 100% عن المباراة بسبب استقبال هدف، لكن الأهم هو حصد النقاط الثلاث. #الشباب…

items.summary: تصويت يثير الجدل
items.body: تصويت يثير الجدل كشف تصويت الصحفي البرتغالي أنطونيو تاديا في جائزة الكرة الذهبية لعام 2026 عن اختيارات لافتة، بعدما منح صدارة قائمته للإسباني لامين يامال، متجاهلًا وضع الفائز بالجائزة هاري كين في مركز متقدم، ومفضلًا عليه عددًا من النجوم، بينما جاء الأرجنتيني ليونيل ميسي في المركز السابع. ووضع تاديا نجم برشلونة الشاب في المرتبة الأولى، يليه الفرنسي كيليان مبابي، ثم النرويجي إيرلينج هالاند، فيما احتل الجورجي خفيتشا كفاراتسخيليا المركز الرابع، وجاء الإسباني باو كوبارسي خامسًا، بينما اكتفى كين بالمركز السادس، متقدمًا بمركز واحد على ميسي. ولم تتوقف المفاجآت عند هذا الحد، إذ ضمت القائمة البرتغالي نونو مينديز في المركز الثامن، والأرجنتيني لاوتارو مارتينيز تاسعًا، والإسباني رودري عاشرًا، في تصويت عكس تفضيلات الصحفي البرتغالي بشأن أبرز نجوم الموسم. وعلى مستوى الحضور البرتغالي في الترتيب النهائي، جاء فيتينيا في المركز الرابع عشر برصيد 59 نقطة، ليكون أفضل لاعبي بلاده، تلاه جواو نيفيز في المركز التاسع عشر بـ15 نقطة، ثم نونو مينديز في المركز الثالث والعشرين بـ8 نقاط، وبرونو فرنانديز في المركز السابع والعشرين بـ5 نقاط.

And the researchers found that doing this is surprisingly easy, after training participants to do exactly that using virtual reality (VR) twice a week for just one month. items.title: Nearly 30% of US adults admit to lying about or exaggerating their symptoms to get antibiotics from doctors, survey finds
items.summary: In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.
items.body: Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf. "As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder , a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings . However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance , in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017 . items.title: Could AI ever build itself? Scientists map the road to the 'last AI built by humans.'
items.summary: Researchers hope recursive self-improvement could tackle the skyrocketing costs of developing advanced AI models. But is it viable?
items.body: Scientists in China are exploring what it would take to develop "the last AI built by humans" — a powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of creating its own successors. In a new paper, researchers examine how approaches to recursive self-improvement (RSI) could help tackle the rising financial and computational costs of developing ever-more advanced AI models. RSI refers to the idea that future AI models could direct their own training and development, using what they learn from each round of improvements to guide subsequent rounds of development. This recursive feedback loop could eventually enable AI systems to develop newer, more powerful generations of models with minimal human input. The study, which was uploaded to the preprint database arXiv Sept. 10 but has not been peer-reviewed, proposes a framework for classifying AI systems based on their self-improvement capabilities, from Level 1 (lowest) to Level 5 (highest). Rubin Observatory has found what might be a tiny new world in the far reaches of our solar system, hidden beyond the orbit of Neptune — and it is among the largest and brightest objects ever discovered beyond Neptune. If confirmed, the miniature world would increase the number of officially recognized solar system dwarf planets to six. Upper estimates of the object's size place it at more than half the diameter of Pluto, the largest known dwarf planet. "My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Matthew Holman , an astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory and member of the Rubin team who wrote the code that helped discover the prospective dwarf planet, said in a statement . "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong." Hidden among stars The potential dwarf planet, designated 2026 ED138 , orbits the sun at roughly 46 times the distance between Earth and the sun. items.body: On the last day of an ecology field trip to Virginia's Eastern Shore, a biology undergraduate student discovered more than she expected. While searching for shark teeth, Brooklyn Rolph, a student at Mary Baldwin University in Virginia, stumbled upon a stone spearpoint estimated to be around 4,500 years old. "Wow, this is so crazy," Rolph said in a statement . Already primed to look for pointy objects underwater, Rolph found a stone spear and immediately alerted the professors running the trip. "They were ecstatic," she recalled. The stone artifact is about 6 inches (15 centimeters) long and, according to local archaeologists, a type known as a Lehigh/Koens-Crispin point. This kind of stone tool was made by Indigenous people across the East Coast of the U.S. from around 4,500 to 3,000 years ago. Sometimes called a "broadspear," the stone point also may have been used as a knife by prehistoric hunter-gatherers in the Late Archaic period . The stone point is likely 3,000 to 4,500 years old. items.title: Neanderthal DNA still survives in our human family tree. What were our ancient relatives' relationships like?
items.summary: Developing research suggests that ancient interbreeding wasn't random — it was socially patterned, directional and far more complicated than the headlines suggest.
items.body: Deep in a limestone cave on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, two very different sets of humans left behind nearly identical traces of their lives — similar stone tools, the remains of the same prey animals, the same types of seashells pierced and strung into ornaments. They may have been separated by thousands of years and may not have directly interacted. Yet the overlap between them was striking enough that researchers studying the site had to look twice. The site, Üçağızlı II, offers one of the clearest examples of a conundrum that scientists have long wrestled with: Neanderthals and modern humans ( Homo sapiens ) didn't just collide and go their separate ways. They inhabited the same areas, and, as dozens of genetic studies have confirmed, had sex, across tens of thousands of years and on multiple continents. The DNA of nearly every person alive outside Africa today carries the proof: Roughly 2% of the non-African genome is Neanderthal. And yet, there is not a single archaeological site that shows them living together. Knowing that modern humans and Neanderthals mated is not the same as understanding how it happened. items.body: Scientists are getting a new glimpse of how the first galaxies came to be. In a stunning new simulation, researchers charted the aftermath of the universe's "dark age," including the appearance of the first galaxies that began to shine about 380,000 years after the Big Bang . Lumina, the program behind the simulation, catalogs 2 billion years of cosmic time and represents a decent chunk of the 13.8 billion-year-old history of our universe. The results were published Monday (Oct. 26) in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society . "Other simulations cannot zoom in as far as this," study co-author Mark Vogelsberger , a professor of physics at MIT, said in a statement . "The difference between the smallest and largest scales that we simulate is larger than in any other simulation." A video published alongside the paper shows what the scientists saw. The team zoomed in on an area roughly 1.6 billion light-years wide to learn more about how the ingredients of space create galaxies. items.body: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals. Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century. items.body: Colorectal cancer rates have been rising in people under 50 since the mid-1990s. These early-onset cancers tend to be more aggressive and resistant to treatment than cancers in older adults — and now, scientists may be learning why. A new study published Thursday (Oct. 29) in the journal Nature Medicine compared colorectal tumors from people between 29 and over 90 years old, and it revealed key differences between young and old patients. The new findings might, in turn, help scientists uncover new ways to fight colorectal cancer in young people, said study co-author Ana Anderson , a professor of neurology at Harvard Medical School and a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women's Hospital. "I believe that our study is essentially a turning point now in the field," Anderson told Live Science. "Because up until now, we've had more questions than answers." items.title: Bronze Age sword discovered in an Italian lake is still sharp after 3,300 years
items.summary: Archaeologists found several ancient weapons, intact vases and a bronze razor in the volcanic crater lake.
items.body: Archaeologists have recovered a well-preserved bronze sword from a volcanic lake in Italy. The 3,300-year-old weapon may have been deposited in the lake as an offering to a deity or for a high-status warrior who lived long before the rise of the Etruscans or the Romans. The sword was found in Lake Mezzano, which is located in the crater of an ancient volcano roughly 60 miles (100 kilometers) northwest of Rome , according to a translated statement from the Superintendence of Archaeology, Fine Arts and Landscape for the Province of Viterbo and Southern Etruria. Dating to the Late Bronze Age (14th to 13th centuries B.C.), the sword has maintained its sharp edge. It is the third such sword found in Lake Mezzano in the past 50 years. Bronze Age people erected pile dwellings or stilt houses in what is now Lake Mezzano, and archaeologists recovered parts of the submerged settlement during their recent investigations. According to the statement, researchers also found numerous intact vases, axes, arrowheads, daggers, spearheads, pins and a bronze razor. items.title: IBD may transform neurons in the gut, triggering pain even when inflammation is under control
items.summary: A new study with data from mice and human tissues suggests that, in ulcerative colitis, immune cells in the gut might make pain-sensing nerves hypersensitive.
items.body: People with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) experience gut pain that can be severe, and it doesn't always go away when their inflammation is under control and their colonoscopy looks normal. Now, in a new laboratory study, researchers found a previously unknown pain pathway that may explain this phenomenon. The findings, published Oct. 23 in the journal Science Immunology , also point to a potential way to block that pain. "Inflammation in the gut has always been thought of like a fire: the sensory nerves alarm because of the smoke and the heat, and when the fire is put out the alarm should stop," said study co-author Dr. Heng Xu , a physician at Ninth People's Hospital in Shanghai. Xu and his colleagues set out to try to isolate what could be causing the pain even when there's no visible "fire" or "smoke." "What we found is that the tissue itself changes consistency," Xu told Live Science in an email. "It becomes stiff and less elastic, a bit like a scar, and that stiffness alone keeps triggering the alarm even after the fire is out." items.title: Our extinct cousins the Denisovans had a 'distinctive' appearance, new analysis reveals
items.summary: Paleoproteomic analysis of fossils from northern China reveals that Denisovans had a distinctive physical appearance.
items.body: The enigmatic and now-extinct Denisovans of China shared traits with Neanderthals, modern humans and Homo erectus , according to a new study that looked at ancient proteins and fossils. But the Denisovans also had several unique skull traits and genetic variants that made them a distinctive ancient human group, according to the researchers ‪—‬ and these traits have now revealed a new face for a Denisovan man. In the study, published Oct. 21 in the journal Nature , researchers analyzed Denisovan skulls from the archaeological site of Xujiayao in northern China. The Denisovans were a group of ancient humans who lived in Asia and disappeared around 30,000 years ago. This human relative was first identified in 2010 from the DNA of a finger bone discovered in a cave in Siberia. The Xujiayao bones and teeth were excavated in the late 1970s, long before scientists knew about the existence of Denisovans, and were initially thought to be either Neanderthals or archaic Homo sapiens due to the shape of the fossils and their age: 138,000 to 199,000 years old. items.title: A woman carried a 'stone baby' in her abdomen for 3 years
items.summary: A woman's unexplained abdominal pain led doctors to a diagnosis that has only been documented a few hundred times over the past 400 years.
items.body: The patient: A 42-year-old woman in Somaliland, Africa The symptoms: The woman went to the hospital after having three years of chronic, dull pain in her lower abdomen, as well as a growing sense of heaviness in her abdomen that had worsened in recent months. When doctors reviewed her medical history, they learned that, three years earlier, she had experienced a number of symptoms that seemed to indicate a pregnancy. She recalled her abdomen growing over time and feeling "fetal movements," her doctors noted in a report of the case . Then, the movements stopped, the abdominal growth halted, and the enlargement gradually subsided. She had not sought medical care during or after this apparent pregnancy. What happened next: When doctors physically examined the woman's abdomen, they found a hard, irregular mass that extended to her belly button and barely moved when they touched it. Blood tests showed mild anemia, meaning she had fewer healthy red blood cells than normal. Her white blood cell count and kidney and liver tests were normal, and a pregnancy test was negative. items.title: Universities should not be adopting AI to automate their own absurdities
items.summary: The promise of AI automation to fix the administrative problems facing universities is a fallacy. These systems will only increase the burdens of already-struggling institutions says Akhil Barwadj.
items.body: Universities are at a critical point as students and faculty embrace the use of AI. Already, universities like Harvard are introducing courses that feature an AI avatar as an "instructor ." The promises AI offers higher education are familiar: an increase in efficiency as a consequence of less administration, more teaching coverage, better feedback and smarter assessment. But introducing artificial intelligence (AI) systems in an attempt to fix these problems is not the answer. If anything, AI systems will magnify and speed up the bureaucracy that is driving universities' decline. In practice, the more likely outcome is darker: AI will not simply sweep away the bureaucratic machinery of universities; it will give that machinery a new regime of AI compliance — more policies, more forms, more trackers, more oversight roles and more work downloaded onto faculty who are already stretched thin. The danger is not that AI will destroy universities but that universities will use AI to preserve the very processes that make them dysfunctional. Previously, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommended that all newborns be vaccinated against HBV within hours of birth ‪—‬ a strategy known as "universal birth-dose vaccination." items.body: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers. Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover. The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look. A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how. That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business. items.title: Watch the full 'Hunter's Moon' rise next to Saturn this weekend
items.summary: You'll have two chances to see October's full Hunter's Moon rise dramatically this week. Here's when to get the best views.
items.body: October's full "Hunter's Moon" is about to rise, and skywatchers will get two great chances to see it appear on the eastern horizon around sunset. Although it officially turns full at 12:11 a.m. EDT on Monday (Oct. 26), the Hunter's Moon will appear almost perfectly full as it rises on both Sunday (Oct. 25) and Monday evenings, giving skywatchers two opportunities to observe it. October's full moon is nicknamed the Hunter's Moon because it was traditionally a signal for hunters to prepare for the coming cold winter by hunting, slaughtering and preserving meat, according to Time and Date . That's an Anglo-Saxon name; Native American names for October's full moon include the Drying Rice Moon, the Falling Leaves Moon and the Freezing Moon. items.title: Why were the Nazca Lines built?
items.summary: The Nazca Lines are sprawling geoglyphs that were constructed on Peru's ground and hillsides around 2,000 years ago. But why were they built?
items.body: The Nazca Lines are the most famous geoglyphs in the world. Dating back around 2,000 years and reaching a combined length of more than 800 miles (1,300 kilometers), they depict a variety of motifs, including humans, animals, geometric shapes, plants and flowers. These designs were constructed on the arid hills and valleys of coastal Peru by the Nazca people between 200 B.C. and A.D. 500, long before writing was used in the region. It's not clear exactly how many Nazca Lines there are, but they number in the thousands, with new geoglyphs continuing to be discovered with the help of AI . But why were the Nazca Lines built? Scientists have been debating this question since the lines were first formally investigated in the early 20th century. Although the definite answer remains unknown, experts have proposed various reasons for the famous geoglyphs. There "are many ideas out there about their function and meaning," Ana Nieves , a professor of art history at Northeastern Illinois University, told Live Science in an email. In the wake of that revelation, she's been left without a diagnosis, and she said on a podcast that she felt she was "back at square one, where I don't know what's going on with me." Applegate's case is not totally unique, although MS diagnosis has improved over the years. Studies offer different estimates of how frequently MS is misdiagnosed, with rates ranging from 5% to over 40%, depending on the patient population and clinical setting. There is also some degree of underdiagnosis — cases in which people with MS aren't flagged as having the disease. So, how difficult is MS to identify, and what does that mean for patients? Live Science spoke with experts about the current state of MS diagnostics and the improvements that may be coming in the future. items.summary: Tesla recently demonstrated its Rocket Roadster "flying car." We asked our readers whether they think flying cars will be widely available in the near future.
items.body: Last week, Tesla unveiled a new "flying" edition of its Roadster electric vehicle. While some experts remain skeptical that the new "Rocket" EV is feasible in the real world , the demonstration reignited a long-standing debate about whether flying cars could soon become a reality . In response to this demonstration, Live Science polled its readers on whether they think flying cars will be available to consumers in the next five years. Over 280 readers responded, with the largest voting group, 34% of readers, picking "No, we need more than five years for flying cars to take off." The next-highest voting bloc was even more skeptical with 23% of readers choosing "No, flying cars will never happen." Several comments reflected this pessimistic view, with one commenter leaving this response: "No flying cars. In my almost 60 years of driving experience I find that most people can't handle driving in 2 dimensions let alone 3. Besides that we have face [sic] so many other problems: hunger, poverty, inadequate healthcare, the careless disregard for our planet. What are we leaving my grandchildren and great grandchildren??" items.body: With artificial intelligence (AI), scientists have a powerful new tool for creating never-before-seen proteins, which can be used to make either groundbreaking new medicines or devastating bioweapons. To help guard against nefarious uses of these proteins, scientists have recently figured out a way to "watermark" them without compromising their function. A team from Google DeepMind developed this technique to better track the provenance of AI-designed proteins. "This has the potential to reduce biosecurity threats, such as unauthorized toxin creation, and may help with database curation, preventing artificial designs from cluttering the standard databases," said Roy Sleator , a biology professor at Munster Technological University in Ireland, who was not involved in the research. "In practice, it could help trace a design's origin, flag engineered proteins for extra biosecurity checks, and reduce misleading claims about how a protein was made," Sleator told Live Science in an email. However, in its current form, the same AI technologies that add watermarks can also strip them away, other experts warned. items.body: Crows are intelligent animals that can use tools , hold grudges and even host funerals . Now, new research suggests these birds can make certain decisions faster than humans and monkeys — another potential sign of their smarts, the researchers argue. In a study published Thursday (Oct. 22) in the journal Science , researchers found that two carrion crows ( Corvus corone ) could distinguish the direction of moving dots on a screen in an average of 235 milliseconds, or less than a quarter of a second. By contrast, historical studies of humans suggest they make decisions in similar tasks six seconds as fast. The birds were highly accurate, and recordings of their brain activity suggested that their decision-making process resembled that seen in primates and humans. Given birds and mammals have evolved along separate paths for more than 310 million years , "this suggests that evolution may have independently developed similar solutions to the same computational problem," study co-author Andreas Nieder , a professor of animal physiology and director of the Institute of Neurobiology at the University of Tübingen in Germany, told Live Science in an email. items.title: Brain scans reveal 'number line' that's used to mentally compare values
items.summary: Although whole numbers and fractions are processed differently in the brain, when you compare their values, a single "mental map" akin to a number line lights up.
items.body: Picture a number line, with the values running from the smallest to the largest. New research shows that the human brain uses a similar system when comparing numbers; in the study, scientists uncovered a "mental map" in which numbers have unique coordinates in the brain, which may help us place them in order of magnitude. "Numbers are abstract concepts, but our brains have ways of organizing them that allow us to compare and reason about their values," said study co-authors Daniela Valério , a postdoctoral researcher in the INSERM-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit (UNICOG) in France, and Stanislas Dehaene , the director of UNICOG. "What is fascinating is that the brain can bring together numbers that look very different, such as integers [whole numbers] and fractions, within a common system," they told Live Science in a joint statement. items.body: Cryptic snakes in Southeast Asia have evolved a remarkable trick for evading predators: Instead of slithering, they arch their long bodies and tumble away at high speeds. The dwarf reed snakes ( Pseudorabdion ) pull off this acrobatic feat by keeping their head in a relatively fixed position while rotating the rest of their body, according to a new study published Monday (Oct. 19) in the journal Current Biology . Researchers filmed the snakes from different angles to better understand the mechanics of the rolling, or cartwheeling, behavior. They found that the snakes were capable of reaching velocities of up to 12.1 feet per second (3.69 meters per second), which is much faster than they can slither (technically referred to as undulating locomotion). "Rolling allows them to escape from danger very quickly," study first author Yosuke Kojima , a lecturer in the biology department at Toho University in Japan, told Live Science. The historic endeavor marks another major step toward humanity's shared goal of understanding — and perhaps eventually colonizing — one of our closest planetary neighbors , experts say. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA) Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) probe is an international effort, constructed with help from NASA, the European Space Agency (ESA) and others. Over the next few years, it will closely study the Red Planet's twin moons, Phobos and Deimos . The spacecraft will snap close-up photos of the pair before attempting to land on the larger satellite, Phobos, to scoop up rocky material that will hopefully be carried back to Earth in around five years. If the mission is successful, the returned samples will finally settle a decades-old mystery about the origins of both moons. The findings could also help paint a picture of Mars' ancient history and provide clues about what the early solar system was like. items.title: Will plants survive climate change? The 'Great Dying' reveals clues about their resilience.
items.summary: Plants can't easily pick up and move when environmental conditions get rough, so they've evolved strategies to weather harsh conditions in place. That could help some plants survive in the face of a warming climate.
items.body: About 251 million years ago, volcanic eruptions wiped out most life on Earth. For about a million years , the Siberian Traps in Russia spewed huge clouds of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, leading to the most severe extinction event in our planet's history. Equatorial temperatures spiked , making much of the land too hot for life. Meanwhile, the oceans became acidic and most of the creatures in them suffocated from lack of oxygen . Known as the Permian-Triassic mass extinction or the "Great Dying," it ultimately destroyed more than 90% of ocean life and 70% of terrestrial species . However, in a corner of what is now China, a refuge of pollen-producing plants avoided that fate and created an oasis for surviving animals. Research suggests that this was not the only place where plants were able to weather catastrophic climate change during the Great Dying, and that plants may have been better able to withstand the extinction event than other organisms. items.body: Climate change is making Earth progressively rounder, new research finds. The findings are a signal of human-caused climate change, however, and tracking the shape of the Earth can help reveal just how much impact people are having on its ice caps. Our planet is not a perfect sphere. Because of its rotation, it is a bit flatter at the poles and bulges in the middle. But the new study reveals that Earth is getting rounder at an accelerated rate, largely due to shifts caused by the melting polar ice caps. This finding applies only to the solid parts of the planet; the ocean continues to bulge outward at the equator. The study, published Sept. 9 in the journal JGR Solid Earth , used direct measurements from the global navigation satellite system (GNSS) to track the planet's shape-shifting over time. This system provides direct measurements, but there are limits in how it can be used. For example, there are few GNSS stations near the North and South poles and few in remote oceans because they must be deployed on buoys. Researchers revealed the four states that together make up the Upper Basin — Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming — lost almost twice as much groundwater as the Lower Basin did during an intense drought in the southwestern U.S. between 2020 and 2022. items.title: حفل زفاف يتحول لفضيحة في مصر.. السبب "مأذون مزيف"

items.title: عضتا قرش تقتلان مسنة في جنوب إفريقيا

items.title: علم يثير غضبا في جامعة موسكو.. والجيش الصيني يتحرك

items.title: صورة تذكارية تتحول لمشهد مرعب.. تمساح يقتل صيادا في فلوريدا
items.summary: تحولت لحظات مثيرة عاشها صياد أميركي مسن بعد اصطياده سمكة من إحدى بحيرات ولاية فلوريدا إلى مأساة مروعة، بعدما باغته تمساح ضخم وجره إلى المياه أمام أنظار أشخاص كانوا في الموقع، قبل أن يفارق الحياة.

items.title: ثعابين بحرية قبالة كاليفورنيا.. ماذا حدث؟

items.title: مولود جديد..فرحة ونفقات قد تربك الأسرة

items.title: شواهد قبور تسخر من أحداث 2026 في ملبورن

items.title: مغادرة حاملة طائرات عملاقة تتحول إلى حدث شعبي في بريطانيا

items.summary: أظهر مقطع فيديو متداول على مواقع التواصل الاجتماعي سيدة تتوسل إلى مجموعة من الملثمين لعدم اقتحام متجرها ونهبه، وذلك خلال احتجاجات واسعة النطاق تخللتها أعمال عنف.

items.title: مسؤول محبوس وتحقيقات مستمرة.. قضية بيانات تهز مصر

items.title: من المهربين إلى الغابة.. غوريلا تبدأ حياة جديدة في البرية
items.summary: لم تكن الغوريلا الصغيرة "بيلي" تدرك أن رحلتها القصيرة ستستغرق سنوات، بعدما انتزعها مهربون من موطنها الطبيعي وهي رضيعة، لتصبح إحدى ضحايا تجارة غير قانونية قيمتها عالميا 20 مليار دولار سنويا.

items.title: "أظهر تحسنا".. الفاتيكان يكشف تطورات حالة البابا بعد الجراحة
items.summary: قال الفاتيكان، الجمعة، إن البابا ليو يظهر تحسنا مطردا في المستشفى، بعد خضوعه يوم الثلاثاء الماضي لعملية جراحية لاستئصال ورم سرطاني في الرئة.

items.title: "IMI" ترفض تقرير هيئة تنظيم الاتصالات البريطانية

items.title: كوب شاي يفضح جريمة محتملة.. طالبة صينية متهمة بتسميم زميلها
items.summary: قاد طعم غير معتاد في كوب شاي إلى كشف شبهة تسميم داخل جامعة وايومنغ الأميركية، انتهت بتوقيف طالبة دراسات عليا صينية في مطار لوس أنجلوس، أثناء محاولتها مغادرة الولايات المتحدة.

items.title: اللوفر تحت خطر الإغلاق

items.title: أستراليا.. كاميرا في أماكن استحمام النساء على سفينة عسكرية

items.title: الفاتيكان يكشف الحالة الصحية للبابا ليو بعد خضوعه للجراحة
items.summary: أعلن الفاتيكان، الأربعاء، أن البابا ليو الرابع عشر تناول طعامه بشكل طبيعي وبدأ المشي وأداء تمارين التنفس، مشيرا إلى أن فحوصاته الطبية بعد العملية الجراحية التي خضع لها لاستئصال ورم سرطاني من رئته جاءت طبيعية.

items.title: 55 ألف سرقة يوميا.. متاجر بريطانيا تنزف المليارات
items.summary: تتصاعد المخاوف في بريطانيا من انتشار سرقات المتاجر، وسط تقديرات تشير إلى وقوع نحو 55 ألف حادثة يوميا، وخسائر سنوية بمليارات الجنيهات الإسترلينية، في وقت يثير فيه تفاقم الظاهرة تساؤلات بشأن فعالية القوانين وقدرة الشرطة على مكافحتها.

items.title: اعتداءات جنسية بحضانة في لندن.. وشكوى سابقة تثير غضب الأسر
items.summary: طالبت عائلات أطفال تعرضوا لاعتداءات جنسية بحضانة في لندن بتحقيق مستقل وعاجل، بعدما كشفت صحيفة "غارديان" البريطانية أن الموظف المسؤول عن الاعتداءات سمح له بالعودة إلى العمل رغم شكوى أثارت مخاوف بشأنه قبل عام من تصويره اعتداءات على طفلات في رعايته.

items.title: 6 وفيات و7 مصابين بانهيار عقار في القاهرة

items.title: في سابقة من نوعها.. إسرائيل تعيد قطعا أثرية إلى اليونان

items.title: هجوم إلكتروني يستهدف أنظمة التبريد في مئات المتاجر الفرنسية

items.title: بعد استئصال ورم من الرئة.. الفاتيكان يكشف حالة البابا
items.summary: أعلن الفاتيكان الثلاثاء أن العملية الجراحية التي خضع لها البابا ليو الرابع عشر في مستشفى جيميلي بروما لاستئصال ورم من رئته قد "أجريت بنجاح".

items.title: جر نفسه للمرحاض.. تعويض لرجل من أصحاب الهمم في بريطانيا

items.title: عمرها 14 ألف عام.. أستراليا تعيد إلى الأردن قطعة أثرية نادرة

items.title: من أحياء أوغندا الفقيرة إلى العالمية.. قصة "غيتو كيدز"
